rw: GDP is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period. It is the main measure of the size of an economy.

ww.The total amount of money held by the go: The government's cash holdings are a measure of public finance. GDP counts everything a country produces, not what its government holds.
ww.The number of people who live in the cou: Population is a head count of residents. GDP measures output, not how many people live in the country.
ww.The average price of consumer goods in t: The average price of goods is shown by a price index such as the CPI. GDP measures output, not price levels.

rw: Cheaper loans encourage firms and households to borrow and spend more. This is why central banks cut rates to boost a slow economy.

ww.Borrowing and spending tend to decrease: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so borrowing and spending tend to rise. A decrease is the opposite of what usually follows.
ww.Neither borrowing nor spending changes: Rates change the cost of credit, so behavior changes too. Borrowing and spending usually react to a rate cut instead of staying put.
ww.Borrowing stops while spending doubles: Borrowing does not stop when rates fall. A cut makes loans cheaper, so borrowing normally rises, and spending does not double.

rw: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. Each dollar then buys less, so purchasing power falls.

ww.An increase in the number of workers: More workers is about the labor force. Inflation is about prices, so a rising number of workers does not define it.
ww.A rise in the price of one product only: A rise in the price of one product is a relative price change. Inflation is a broad rise across most goods and services.
ww.A general decrease in prices over time: A general fall in prices is deflation, the opposite of inflation. Inflation is when the price level rises.

rw: Perfect competition has many sellers of near-identical products, and no seller can set the price. The market sets it, so each firm is a price taker.

ww.Oligopoly market: An oligopoly has a few large sellers who influence price. The scenario has many sellers and none with price power.
ww.Duopoly of two firms: A duopoly has just two sellers. The scenario describes many sellers, so a duopoly does not fit.
ww.A single monopoly firm: A monopoly has one seller with price power. The scenario has many sellers and none with control, so it is the opposite.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best option given up. Every choice has one, since time and money are limited.

ww.The total price paid for an item at the: The price paid is a money cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, whether or not money changes hands.
ww.The cost of insurance that covers an ite: Insurance cost is a money expense. Opportunity cost is about the best option forgone, not what protection costs.
ww.The cost of an item after a sale discoun: A discounted price is still the money paid. Opportunity cost measures what you give up by choosing one option over another.

rw: Self-awareness is recognizing your own emotions and how they shape your behavior. It helps you respond well and choose your actions.

ww.Avoiding every stressful situation that: Avoiding stress is avoidance, not insight. Self-awareness means understanding your emotions rather than running from situations.
ww.Predicting what other people will do nex: Predicting others' actions is social awareness or guesswork. Self-awareness is about knowing your own feelings and their effects.
ww.Hiding your feelings from all of your co: Hiding feelings is suppression. Self-awareness means admitting what you feel, which is the first step to managing it.

rw: Self-regulation is controlling emotions and impulses before reacting. Walking away to calm down before replying prevents an angry response.

ww.Self-promotion: Self-promotion means drawing attention to your own achievements. Taking a walk to cool down has nothing to do with it.
ww.Competitiveness: Competitiveness is wanting to outdo others. The worker is calming down, not trying to win, so it is not the skill shown.
ww.Procrastination: Procrastination is putting off a task without a good reason. The walk is a short, deliberate pause to manage emotion, and the worker still replies.

rw: Empathy is understanding and sharing another person's feelings. It lets you respond with care and strengthens relationships at work.

ww.Agreeing with every opinion that others: Agreeing with every opinion is people-pleasing. You can show empathy for someone's feelings without agreeing with their views.
ww.Giving orders to coworkers calmly each d: Giving orders is a leadership act. Empathy is about understanding feelings, not directing people.
ww.Ignoring emotions to focus on tasks alon: Ignoring emotions is the opposite of empathy. Empathy requires noticing and caring about how others feel.

rw: Asking how you can help and listening shows empathy. It tells the coworker you care and lets you offer help that fits their need.

ww.Avoiding them until the busy period has: Avoiding someone who is overwhelmed leaves them alone with the problem. Empathy means showing up when a coworker needs support.
ww.Giving them more tasks to prove their st: Piling on more tasks adds to the stress and ignores their situation. It shows no concern for how they feel.
ww.Telling them everyone has problems and m: Saying everyone has problems and moving on dismisses their feelings. Empathy means pausing to acknowledge and support them.

rw: Conflict management helps people resolve disagreement. Letting both explain and suggesting a compromise uses social awareness, noticing and respecting each person's view.

ww.Avoidance by staying out of the conflict: Avoidance means staying out of the conflict. The third member steps in to help, so avoidance is not what is shown.
ww.Manipulation by choosing sides in secret: Manipulation means influencing others in a sneaky way. The third member listens openly and does not take sides in secret.
ww.Self-promotion by taking charge for cred: Self-promotion seeks credit. The third member is helping settle the dispute for the team's sake, not for personal recognition.

rw: Emotional intelligence improves communication, teamwork and decision making. People who read and manage emotions well work better together.

ww.It guarantees that no conflicts happen a: EI cannot guarantee that no conflicts happen. It helps people handle them well, but disagreements still occur at work.
ww.It replaces technical skills for any job: EI does not replace technical skills. Most jobs need both knowledge of the work and the ability to work well with people.
ww.It removes the need for any rules at wor: EI does not remove the need for rules. It helps people follow and work within them, but organizations still need guidelines.

rw: Short breaks restore energy, and prioritizing tasks makes the workload manageable. Both are healthy ways to cope with stress.

ww.Blaming coworkers for every single probl: Blaming coworkers does not reduce stress. It damages trust and leaves the real problems unresolved.
ww.Skipping meals to finish tasks faster ea: Skipping meals harms health and focus. It makes stress worse and tasks slower, not faster, in the long run.
ww.Ignoring all deadlines until the last da: Ignoring deadlines until the last day piles up pressure. It increases stress and the chance of mistakes or missed work.

rw: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on its risks in the hope of profit. They organize resources, make decisions and accept possible losses.

ww.A person who only invests money in other: Someone who only invests in other firms is an investor. An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and carries its risks.
ww.A person who regulates businesses for th: A person who regulates businesses is a government official. Entrepreneurs run businesses rather than oversee them.
ww.A person who works for a fixed salary in: A person with a fixed salary is an employee. Entrepreneurs earn profit, which can rise or fall, and bear the risk.

rw: A business plan states goals and how the business will reach them. It guides decisions and helps win support from lenders and investors.

ww.To list the daily tasks of employees onl: Employee tasks are only a small piece of operations. A business plan covers markets, finances and strategy as well.
ww.To replace the need for financial record: A business plan does not replace financial records. It includes projections, but the firm still needs actual books.
ww.To keep the business idea secret from ev: A plan is shared with lenders, partners and staff, not hidden. Its purpose is to communicate how the business will succeed.

rw: Personal savings are a common source of start-up funding. The owner invests their own money, which avoids debt and shows commitment.

ww.Customers' credit card numbers: Customers' card numbers are private data used to pay for goods. They are not a source of money for funding a startup.
ww.Government tax refund checks: Tax refunds go to taxpayers and are not a typical business funding source. They are small and unreliable for a startup.
ww.Profits from future sales of goods: Future sales do not exist yet. A new business cannot spend profits it has not earned, so it needs other funding to start.

rw: Entrepreneurs can lose the money they invest if the business fails. Accepting this risk is part of starting a business.

ww.Guaranteed profit in the first month of: Profit in the first month is not guaranteed. Many new businesses lose money at first while they build a customer base.
ww.Complete protection from competition for: No business is protected from competition. Rivals can enter the market at any time, so competition is a constant risk.
ww.Freedom from all legal duties and from p: Businesses must obey laws and pay taxes. There is no freedom from these duties for entrepreneurs.

rw: Market research and testing the idea with potential customers show whether people will pay her prices. It lowers risk before she spends big.

ww.Hire a large team of staff before the ca: Hiring a big team before knowing if customers will pay adds costs with no proof of demand. It puts Mina at greater financial risk.
ww.Sign a long lease on a building before r: Signing a long lease before researching demand locks her into high costs. If customers do not come, she is stuck paying rent.
ww.Set prices at random and simply hope for: Setting prices at random and hoping is guesswork. Prices should rest on costs and what customers will pay.

rw: A USP explains how a business is different from competitors and why customers should choose it. It highlights a clear advantage.

ww.States the legal structure of the firm a: The legal structure is a separate choice, such as sole proprietorship or corporation. A USP is about what sets the business apart.
ww.Lists all of the business's expenses for: Expenses are listed in financial statements. A USP concerns what makes the business stand out, not its costs.
ww.Shows the daily schedule of employees at: An employee schedule is an operations tool. A USP is a marketing idea about what makes the business special.

rw: A franchise is a business that uses a larger company's brand and system under a license. The franchisee pays fees and follows the parent's rules.

ww.Importing goods to sell online to buyers: Importing and selling online is a trade or retail model. It does not involve using another firm's brand and system.
ww.Selling shares of stock to the public on: Selling shares of stock raises money by giving up ownership. It is not a franchise arrangement.
ww.Starting a store with a brand you own ou: A store with a brand you own outright and run alone is an independent business. A franchise relies on another company's brand and system.

rw: Expanding capacity carefully, with staff, equipment or partners, lets the business meet demand without losing quality. Careful growth avoids overstretching.

ww.Hide the delays from buyers and promise: Hiding delays from buyers and promising faster shipping is dishonest. It damages trust and leads to angry customers.
ww.Stop taking any new orders and ignore th: Refusing new orders ignores growth that the business has worked for. It wastes the chance to earn more.
ww.Lower the quality of the product so that: Lowering quality to ship faster hurts the brand. Customers who get a worse product may leave and not return.

rw: Networking builds relationships that can lead to partners, customers, advice and funding. These contacts help a new business grow.

ww.It replaces the need to serve customers: Networking does not replace serving customers. Customers are the source of income, so serving them stays essential.
ww.It removes the need for a business plan: Networking does not remove the need for a business plan. A plan sets direction and is needed whatever contacts you have.
ww.It guarantees that the business will suc: Nothing guarantees success. Networking creates opportunities, but the business still has to deliver value.

rw: An income statement shows revenue and expenses over a period, leading to profit or loss. It tells how a business performed.

ww.Balance sheet: A balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity at one date. It does not cover a period of earning and spending.
ww.Trial balance: A trial balance lists ledger balances to check debits equal credits. It is a bookkeeping check, not a report of performance.
ww.Cash flow report: A cash flow report tracks cash moving in and out. It is not the statement that sets out revenue, expenses and profit.

rw: Net income equals revenue minus expenses. $80,000 minus $62,000 is $18,000.

ww.$80,000: $80,000 is the revenue before expenses. Net income is what remains after subtracting expenses.
ww.$62,000: $62,000 is the expenses. Net income subtracts them from revenue to find profit.
ww.$142,000: $142,000 adds revenue and expenses together. Net income subtracts expenses from revenue, giving $18,000.

rw: The accounting equation says assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. It shows everything the business owns is funded by debt or by the owners.

ww.Assets equal revenue minus expenses for: Revenue minus expenses is net income. The accounting equation links assets, liabilities and equity.
ww.Equity equals debts minus revenue each y: The accounting equation does not subtract revenue from debts. It states that assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity.
ww.Liabilities equal assets plus equity at: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, not the other way round. Here liabilities have been put on the wrong side.

rw: The current ratio equals current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts.

ww.Profit margin: Profit margin compares profit with sales. It does not compare current assets with current liabilities.
ww.Stock turnover: Stock turnover measures how quickly inventory is sold and replaced. It is about goods moving, not about short-term solvency.
ww.Debt ratio: The debt ratio compares total debt with total assets. It looks at all debt, not just current assets and liabilities.

rw: Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. $90,000 divided by $60,000 is 1.5, or 1.5 to 1.

ww.0.67 to 1: 0.67 to 1 turns the formula upside down, liabilities over assets. The current ratio divides assets by liabilities, so it is 1.5.
ww.150 to 1: 150 to 1 is not what the numbers give. $90,000 over $60,000 equals 1.5.
ww.30 to 1: 30 to 1 does not follow from the figures. Dividing $90,000 by $60,000 gives 1.5 to 1.

rw: Profit margin shows the share of sales that becomes profit. A higher margin means more profit from each dollar of sales.

ww.The value of inventory on hand at year e: The value of inventory is on the balance sheet. Profit margin is about profit as a share of sales.
ww.How fast customers pay their bills: How fast customers pay is a measure of receivables collection. It is unrelated to profit margin.
ww.The total amount of debt owed by it: Total debt owed appears among liabilities on the balance sheet. Profit margin is about earnings, not borrowing.

rw: Profit margin equals net income divided by sales. $12,000 divided by $120,000 is 0.10, or 10%.

ww.100%: 100% would mean all sales were profit with no costs. Net income is only a part of sales, so the margin is far lower.
ww.90%: 90% would mean expenses were just 10% of sales. Net income of $12,000 on $120,000 is only 10%.
ww.1%: 1% would need net income of only $1,200 on $120,000 of sales. The actual figure of $12,000 gives 10%.

rw: A budget plans income and spending and helps control costs. Comparing results with the budget shows where to adjust.

ww.To avoid paying any taxes at all in a gi: Budgets do not avoid taxes. Taxes are owed whether or not a firm budgets.
ww.To record transactions after they have h: Recording transactions after they happen is bookkeeping. A budget is a plan made in advance.
ww.To prove to customers that prices are fa: Budgets are internal planning tools. They are not made to prove anything to customers about prices.

rw: Spending $500 over budget is an unfavorable variance. It means the department used more than planned.

ww.A $0 variance because the numbers are cl: Spending of $4,500 against a budget of $4,000 is not close to zero variance. A $500 gap is a real difference.
ww.A $500 favorable variance because spendi: A favorable variance would mean spending came in below plan. Here spending was higher, so it is unfavorable.
ww.A $4,500 profit because the budget was f: $4,500 is the actual spending, not a profit. The budget was not met, since spending exceeded the $4,000 plan.

rw: Break-even is where total revenue equals total costs. Below it a business loses money, and above it a profit begins.

ww.The point where costs are zero for the w: Costs do not drop to zero at break-even. At that point revenue just covers all costs.
ww.The point where profit is at its highest: The highest profit is a different point. Break-even is where profit is exactly zero.
ww.The point where the business has no cust: Having no customers means zero sales and a loss, not break-even. Break-even needs enough sales to cover costs.

rw: A job description lists a position's duties and requirements. It helps with hiring, training and judging performance.

ww.To show the company's yearly profit figu: Profit figures belong in financial statements. A job description is about a role, not the company's yearly results.
ww.To record employee vacation days for the: Vacation days are recorded in HR records. They are not the purpose of a job description.
ww.To list the prices of the company produc: Product prices go in price lists. A job description concerns what a worker does, not what the firm sells.

rw: Paid health insurance is an employee benefit, provided in addition to wages. It helps workers with medical costs.

ww.A fine charged for arriving late to work: A fine for lateness is a penalty, not a benefit. Benefits are extras that the employer gives to help workers.
ww.The employee's regular hourly wage rate: A regular wage is the basic pay for work. Benefits are additional to wages, such as insurance or paid leave.
ww.A job application fee paid by candidates: Candidates do not pay to apply. A fee would be a cost, not a benefit given by the employer.

rw: The main goal of training is to improve skills and job performance. Trained workers are more productive and make fewer errors.

ww.To replace job descriptions of workers: Training does not replace job descriptions. It teaches workers skills, while a description lists duties.
ww.To lower the quality of work done: Training aims to raise the quality of work, not lower it. Well-trained staff do better work.
ww.To increase the number of quitters: Training aims to keep staff, not to make them quit. Good training raises skills and morale.

rw: Meeting privately, discussing expectations and documenting is fair and professional. It gives the employee a chance to explain and creates a record.

ww.Fire the employee at once without any wa: Firing without warning is too harsh for a first step. Most firms start with a conversation and a warning.
ww.Ignore it and hope the employee can work: Ignoring the issue lets it continue. Lateness three times in a month needs a response from the supervisor.
ww.Announce the lateness to the entire staf: Announcing it to the whole staff embarrasses the employee. Performance matters should be handled in private.

rw: Growth opportunities and fair pay make employees want to stay. Turnover falls when people feel valued and see a future.

ww.Raising workloads without more support: Heavier workloads without support cause burnout. That makes employees more likely to leave, not less.
ww.Avoiding feedback to keep things simple: Avoiding feedback leaves workers unsure how they are doing. Unclear expectations often push people to quit.
ww.Cutting training budgets to save money n: Cutting training budgets limits growth and skills. It tends to raise turnover as people look elsewhere for development.

rw: Diversity means differences among staff in background and perspective, such as culture, age, gender and experience. A mix of views can improve ideas and decisions.

ww.Having all employees work only on the ni: Working only the night shift is a schedule, not diversity. Diversity is about differences among people.
ww.Having all employees do the very same ta: Having everyone do the same task is uniformity. Diversity refers to differences among staff, not identical jobs.
ww.Having employees who are all in one age: A staff all in one age group has no diversity of age. Diversity means including a range of people.

rw: A performance appraisal evaluates an employee's work and gives feedback for improvement. It helps set goals and can guide pay or promotion.

ww.To decide which employees to hire for th: Hiring decisions are made through recruitment and selection. An appraisal looks at the work of people already employed.
ww.To announce each employee's pay to the w: Pay is not announced to everyone. An appraisal is a private review between an employee and their manager.
ww.To list the company's products and their: Product lists belong in catalogs. An appraisal is about how an employee is doing.

rw: A database is an organized collection of data that can be searched and updated. Businesses use it to store records such as customers and orders.

ww.A type of business loan from a bank for: A business loan is money borrowed from a bank. It has nothing to do with storing data.
ww.A machine used only for printing documen: A printing machine is a printer. A database stores and organizes data, not paper documents.
ww.A group of employees who work with compu: A group of employees who work with computers is an IT team. A database is a store of information, not a group of people.

rw: Businesses back up data so they can restore it if the original is lost or damaged. This guards against failure, mistakes and attacks.

ww.To avoid ever updating the data on the c: Backups do not stop updating. They are copies of data so that it can be recovered.
ww.To increase the size of the original fil: Backups do not aim to enlarge the original files. They make a separate copy for safekeeping.
ww.To make the data harder for employees to: Backups do not make data harder to use. They run in the background to protect it.

rw: Limiting access to authorized employees keeps customer data safe. People see only the data they need for their jobs.

ww.Emailing customer data to personal accou: Emailing customer data to personal accounts moves it outside the company's control. That raises the risk of a leak.
ww.Storing records in an unlocked public fo: An unlocked public folder lets anyone view the records. Customer data should be kept private and protected.
ww.Sharing passwords with the whole team at: Sharing passwords makes it impossible to tell who accessed data. It also raises the risk of misuse.

rw: Data privacy is protecting personal information from misuse or unauthorized access. It respects people's rights and builds customer trust.

ww.Selling customer data to others without: Selling customer data without telling them breaks privacy. Data privacy means protecting that information.
ww.Posting customer data openly on a public: Posting data on a public website exposes it to anyone. It is a breach of privacy, not protection.
ww.Keeping no records of any kind about its: Privacy does not require having no records. Businesses can keep records if they protect them properly.

rw: An email from 'IT' asking for a password via a link is typically phishing. The right response is not to click and to report it to the real IT team.

ww.Reply with the password in the email to: Replying with a password gives it to an attacker. Real IT departments do not ask for passwords by email.
ww.Click the link and enter the password qu: Clicking the link and entering the password sends credentials to a fake site. The account can then be taken over.
ww.Forward it to all coworkers in the offic: Forwarding the email spreads the threat to others. It should be reported, not shared around the office.

rw: A spreadsheet organizes, calculates and analyzes numerical data. It uses rows, columns and formulas to sum, sort and chart figures.

ww.To scan business documents for computer: Scanning for viruses is the job of antivirus software. A spreadsheet is for working with numbers.
ww.To design logos for the products of the: Logos are made with design software. A spreadsheet is a tool for numbers.
ww.To send marketing messages to customers: Marketing emails are sent with email or marketing tools. A spreadsheet is not made for sending messages.

rw: A survey run with its own customers is primary research. The business collects new data directly for its own purpose.

ww.A competitor's published brochure from t: A competitor's brochure is secondary data, gathered by someone else. Primary research is collected directly by the business.
ww.A government report from last year on tr: A government report is existing information published by others. It is secondary, not primary research.
ww.A magazine article about the industry fr: A magazine article is a published source made by others. That makes it secondary data.

rw: An MIS organizes information to help managers make decisions. It turns data into reports and summaries for planning and control.

ww.To print employee paychecks and nothing: An MIS does much more than print paychecks. It gathers and organizes information for management.
ww.To store only the addresses of customers: An MIS holds many kinds of information, not only customer addresses. Its purpose is to support decision making.
ww.To replace all of the managers in the co: An MIS supports managers and does not replace them. People still make the decisions.

rw: The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion. Together they are the choices a business makes to reach customers.

ww.People, profit, planning and output: People, profit, planning and output are not the marketing mix. The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.
ww.Planning, policy and performance: Planning, policy and performance are not the marketing mix. They are management words, not the four Ps.
ww.Purchase, payment, packaging and price: Purchase, payment, packaging and price are not the four Ps. Only price is part of the marketing mix.

rw: Market segmentation is dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs. It helps a firm target the right people.

ww.One price for all: One price for all is a pricing approach. Segmentation instead splits customers into groups.
ww.Selling the same way: Selling the same way to everyone is mass marketing. Segmentation tailors efforts to groups.
ww.Merging all rivals: Merging rivals is a business combination. It is not about dividing customers into groups.

rw: Target marketing means choosing a specific group of customers to aim at. Serious athletes are the group chosen for this shoe.

ww.Mass production: Mass production makes large quantities of goods. Aiming a shoe at athletes is about choosing a market.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an illegal agreement between rivals to set prices. It has nothing to do with choosing who to sell to.
ww.Market research: Market research gathers information about customers. The company is already acting on what it knows by aiming at athletes.

rw: A social media ad promotes a product by informing and persuading buyers. Promotion is how a business communicates with customers.

ww.Choosing where the product will be sold: Choosing where to sell a product is place. Promotion is about communicating, not distribution.
ww.Setting the price of the product: Setting the price is the price element. It is not a form of promotion.
ww.Designing the product's features: Designing features is product development. Promotion tells people about the product after it is made.

rw: Lowering prices to sell day-old bread adjusts the price element of the marketing mix. It clears stock before it spoils.

ww.Place: Place is where products are sold. Lowering the price of day-old bread does not change where it is sold.
ww.Product: Product covers the item's features and quality. The bread itself is unchanged; only its price changed.
ww.Promotion: Promotion is advertising and publicity. The bakery changed what it charges, not how it advertises.

rw: A brand is a name, symbol or design that identifies a business's products. It sets them apart from others and builds recognition.

ww.The total cost of making one product in: The cost of making a product is a production cost. A brand is how a business and its products are identified.
ww.The list of ingredients that a product c: A list of ingredients is product information. A brand is a name, symbol or design.
ww.The location where a product is sold to: Where a product is sold is its place. A brand is about identity, not location.

rw: Market research helps a company understand customer needs and market conditions. It reduces the risk of poor decisions.

ww.To stop customers from giving opinions a: Research collects customers' opinions, not stops them. It aims to learn what buyers want.
ww.To avoid ever changing their products in: Companies research so they can improve and change products. Avoiding change is the opposite.
ww.To keep prices the same forever for all: Research helps firms set suitable prices, not keep them fixed forever. Markets change.

rw: Customers aged 18 to 24 use social media daily, so short video ads reach them where they are. The plan matches the audience.

ww.Printed flyers mailed to older household: Flyers to older households miss the target group. They would be sent to the wrong people.
ww.Newspaper ads in the retirement section: Retirement-section ads reach older readers, not young adults. They do not fit the audience.
ww.Radio ads late at night in another regio: Late-night radio in another region misses both the age group and the location. It would not reach the customers.

rw: Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale or for use in making products. Managing it well avoids shortages and waste.

ww.Profit earned by the business during the: Profit is what remains after costs. Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds.
ww.Employees who are assigned to a special: Employees on a project are staff, not inventory. Inventory is goods and materials.
ww.Money owed to a business by its credit c: Money owed by credit customers is accounts receivable. It is a different asset from inventory.

rw: The goal of quality control is to ensure products meet standards before they reach customers. It reduces defects and complaints.

ww.To lower the number of products that are: Quality control does not aim to reduce sales. It aims to keep products at a good standard.
ww.To increase the price charged for defect: Defective items should not be sold at higher prices. Quality control tries to find and fix defects.
ww.To avoid checking the products at all be: Quality control involves checking products. Skipping checks would let faults reach customers.

rw: Overstocking ties up money in storage and may force markdowns. The cash cannot be used elsewhere while goods sit.

ww.Faster delivery times to the customers o: Excess inventory does not speed up delivery. The problem is goods that sit unsold.
ww.Higher customer satisfaction from more c: Satisfaction rises when needed goods are available, but having far too many goods is a cost. Unsold stock does not please customers.
ww.Lower storage fees due to bulk buying of: Storing a lot of unsold goods raises storage costs. Buying in bulk does not lower fees when items do not sell.

rw: A supply chain is the network of suppliers, makers and distributors that moves a product to the customer. Each link adds value and affects cost and speed.

ww.A list of all the employees who work for: A list of employees is a staff list. A supply chain is the path a product takes.
ww.A set of financial statements that a com: Financial statements report a company's results. They are separate from the flow of goods.
ww.A chain of retail stores that is owned b: A chain of stores is a retail group. A supply chain is about moving goods from source to customer.

rw: Using more than one supplier gives backup if one factory stops. It spreads risk, so one problem will not halt production.

ww.Ignore supplier problems until they happ: Ignoring supplier problems leaves the firm unprepared. It would suffer the same delay again.
ww.Rely on a single supplier to save on cos: A single supplier saves effort but raises risk. If it fails, the whole production line can stop.
ww.Stop making products that need the part: Stopping production of items that need the part loses sales. It does not manage the risk.

rw: JIT receives goods only as they are needed. It cuts storage costs and waste, but depends on reliable suppliers.

ww.Order extra goods far in advance to buil: JIT does not stockpile in advance. Stockpiling is what it tries to avoid.
ww.Ship the goods to customers only once ea: Shipping once a year in bulk is the opposite of JIT. JIT delivers small amounts when needed.
ww.Hold very large safety stocks at all tim: Holding large safety stocks is the opposite of JIT. JIT aims to keep inventory low.

rw: A safety program aims to prevent accidents and protect employees. Fewer injuries mean fewer costs and a better workplace.

ww.To increase the speed of all tasks at wo: Safety programs do not speed up work. Their goal is to prevent harm, even if that means careful procedures.
ww.To reduce training time for new staff me: Safety programs usually add training. They do not aim to cut training time for new staff.
ww.To replace the need for supervisors at w: Supervisors still guide safe practice. A safety program supports them and does not replace them.

rw: A resume summarizes a person's education, skills and work experience. Employers use it to judge whether to interview someone.

ww.A form that people use to file their yea: A tax form is filed with the tax authority. A resume is a job-seeking document.
ww.A record of expenses that a business has: A record of paid expenses is an accounting record. A resume describes a person's background.
ww.A list of the products that the company: A product list is a catalog. A resume is about a person, not a firm's products.

rw: Arriving on time and meeting commitments shows reliability and respect. These habits build a good reputation.

ww.Using personal phone calls during meetin: Using personal phone calls during meetings shows a lack of focus and respect. It is unprofessional.
ww.Gossiping about coworkers in the break r: Gossiping about coworkers harms trust. It is unprofessional.
ww.Blaming others for your mistakes at work: Blaming others for your mistakes avoids responsibility. Professionals accept accountability.

rw: A mentor is an experienced person who guides someone with less experience. Mentors share advice and help others grow in their careers.

ww.A person who supervises payroll and bene: Someone who handles payroll and benefit records is a payroll or HR clerk. That is not a mentor.
ww.A person who repairs the equipment in th: A person who repairs equipment is a technician. That is a job, not a mentoring role.
ww.A person who orders supplies for the bus: A person who orders supplies is a purchasing clerk. That is a job role, not a mentor.

rw: Researching the company and practicing common questions prepares you well. You can give clear, relevant answers with confidence.

ww.Wait to see which questions come up on t: Waiting to see the questions leaves you unprepared. Preparation improves confidence and answers.
ww.Skip learning about the job requirements: Skipping research on the job and company shows low interest. Employers expect candidates to know the basics.
ww.Memorize one single answer for every que: One memorized answer cannot fit every question. Interviews need answers suited to each question.

rw: A short thank-you note shows appreciation and interest. It leaves a good final impression.

ww.Post details of the interview online for: Posting interview details online can break confidentiality. It looks unprofessional to the employer.
ww.Say nothing and wait for the employer to: Saying nothing misses a chance to follow up. A note keeps you in mind with the employer.
ww.Call the interviewer each day for a week: Calling daily is pushy and annoying. It can hurt your chances.

rw: A career goal is a specific target for a future position or accomplishment. It gives direction and helps you plan steps to get there.

ww.A list of the tasks that are done each d: Daily tasks are part of a job. A career goal is a target for your future.
ww.A record of your past jobs and nothing m: Past jobs are listed on a resume. A career goal looks ahead, not back.
ww.A salary amount that the employer sets f: A salary is pay set by an employer. A career goal is something you choose for yourself.

rw: Skills and industries change, so continuing to learn keeps you employable. It helps you adapt and grow in your career.

ww.Learning stops being useful once a perso: Learning continues to matter at any age. Skills can help people advance or switch careers at any point.
ww.Skills never change at all after graduat: Skills do change after graduation as technology and methods change. Staying current is needed.
ww.Employers do not place any value on new: Employers do value new skills. Workers who keep learning are more useful.

rw: A mission statement states an organization's purpose and what it does. It guides decisions and shows customers and staff what it stands for.

ww.A forecast of the company's sales for th: A forecast predicts sales. A mission statement says why an organization exists.
ww.A list of the duties that employees perf: Duties belong in job descriptions. A mission statement covers the whole organization.
ww.A record of the profits earned in the pa: Profits earned appear in financial reports. A mission statement is about purpose.

rw: SWOT stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. The analysis helps a business plan by looking inside and outside.

ww.Sales, wages, orders and taxes of the fi: Sales, wages, orders and taxes are business figures. SWOT stands for something different.
ww.Stocks, wealth, output and trade of the: Stocks, wealth, output and trade of the nation are economic terms. They are not what SWOT examines.
ww.Suppliers, workers, owners and traders o: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders are groups. SWOT does not examine groups of people.

rw: A new competitor entering the market comes from outside the business. External factors like this are threats or opportunities.

ww.A skilled and loyal staff of workers: A skilled and loyal staff is a strength inside the business. It is an internal factor.
ww.Outdated equipment in the factory plant: Outdated equipment is a weakness inside the business. It is internal, not external.
ww.A strong brand reputation in the market: A strong brand reputation is a strength the business owns. It is internal.

rw: A competitive advantage is a strength that lets a business outperform its rivals. It could be quality, cost, service or brand.

ww.A decrease in the company's prices only: A short-term price cut can be copied by rivals. It is not a lasting advantage.
ww.A law that stops other firms from operat: A law that blocks rival firms is a legal barrier. A competitive advantage comes from a firm's own strengths.
ww.A rule requiring customers to buy from t: A rule requiring customers to buy from one firm would be unfair and illegal. A competitive advantage is earned.

rw: Differentiation means standing out through qualities such as quality and service. Locally roasted beans and friendly service set the shop apart from the chain.

ww.Leaving the market for good and closing: Leaving the market is giving up. The shop is competing by offering something different.
ww.Cost leadership based on the lowest pric: Cost leadership means having the lowest prices. The shop admits it cannot match the chain on price, so it is not using this strategy.
ww.Imitation of the chain's methods and men: Imitation copies a rival's methods. The shop is offering something different instead.

rw: Measurable goals let a business track progress and know when targets are achieved. They keep the team focused and show what needs adjusting.

ww.To prevent employees from knowing what t: Goals are shared so employees know what to aim for. Hiding targets would hurt performance.
ww.To keep goals vague and flexible at all: Vague goals are hard to judge. Measurable goals give clear targets.
ww.To avoid reporting results to the owners: Reporting results is part of accountability. Measurable goals make it possible.

rw: Analyzing the causes and adjusting products, prices or marketing responds to the problem with facts. It aims to win back sales.

ww.Cut all of the advertising budget immedi: Cutting all advertising would likely cut sales further. It does not address the cause.
ww.Ignore the trend and simply wait for sal: Ignoring a falling trend risks more losses. Sales rarely recover without action.
ww.Copy the competitor's logo and name exac: Copying a competitor's logo and name is illegal and unethical. It would not fix the real problem.

rw: A written lease is easier to prove and enforce if a dispute arises. It records the terms, such as rent and length.

ww.A written lease removes the baker's duty: A written lease does not remove the duty to pay rent. It sets out what each party must do.
ww.Oral leases are always illegal in every: Oral leases are not always illegal. Many are valid, but some must be in writing and they are hard to prove.
ww.A written lease lowers the monthly rent: A written lease does not automatically lower rent. It records the rent that was agreed.

rw: A warranty is a promise by a seller about a product's quality or performance. If the product fails, the buyer may be entitled to a repair or refund.

ww.A tax that a seller collects on each sal: A tax collected on sales is a sales tax. A warranty is a promise about a product.
ww.A fee that is paid to the court to start: A fee paid to start a case is a court filing fee. It is not a warranty.
ww.A list of rules about the names of firms: Rules about business names are naming laws. A warranty is a seller's promise.

rw: A partnership agreement sets out how owners share profits, make decisions and handle a departure. It helps settle disputes when someone wants to leave.

ww.A resume of the owners: A resume describes a person's work history. It does not set rules between owners.
ww.A warranty for the firm: A warranty is a promise about a product. It does not cover how owners handle a split.
ww.A sales receipt kept: A sales receipt is a record of one purchase. It does not set rules for the owners.

rw: A debtor is a person who borrows money and must repay it. The lender is the creditor.

ww.Heir: An heir is a person who inherits property. It does not describe someone who borrows money.
ww.Plaintiff: A plaintiff is a person who brings a lawsuit. It is not the term for a borrower.
ww.Creditor: A creditor is the one who lends money and is owed repayment. That is the opposite of a borrower.

rw: A nondisclosure agreement protects confidential business information from being shared. The employee agrees not to reveal secrets such as plans or customer lists.

ww.The employee's right to a raise in pay e: A raise is a pay matter. A nondisclosure agreement concerns secrecy.
ww.The customer's right to a refund of the: A customer's refund right comes from consumer law. An NDA does not cover it.
ww.The company's right to avoid taxes on it: An NDA does not help avoid taxes. It deals with confidentiality, not tax.

rw: Clear and simple language helps readers understand the message and act on it. Confusing writing causes mistakes and delays.

ww.It reduces the need for any reply at all: Clear language does not cut replies. It helps readers understand and respond.
ww.It makes the document look longer on the: Length is not a goal. Clear, simple writing is easier and quicker to read.
ww.It hides the real purpose of the note se: A clear message makes the purpose obvious. It does not hide it.

rw: Open-ended questions invite the customer to explain in their own words. The salesperson learns about needs and preferences and can tailor the pitch.

ww.The pitch becomes much shorter with fewe: Open-ended questions do not shorten a pitch. They invite longer answers.
ww.The customer can only answer yes or no t: Yes or no answers come from closed questions. Open-ended questions allow fuller answers.
ww.The customer is prevented from speaking: Open-ended questions bring the customer into the talk. They do not stop the customer from speaking.

rw: Sending a prompt correction that clearly states the right price fixes the error and keeps trust. It shows honesty and care.

ww.Wait to see if any of the recipients not: Waiting for someone to notice lets a mistake spread. The customer could be misled.
ww.Delete your sent folder and say nothing: Deleting records and staying silent is dishonest. It hides the mistake instead of fixing it.
ww.Blame the client for misreading the orig: Blaming the client is unfair and unprofessional. The error was the sender's.

rw: Tone is the writer's attitude shown through word choice and style. It can sound friendly, formal or rude, and affects how the reader reacts.

ww.The type of font that is used in the mes: Font is a design choice. Tone is about attitude.
ww.The volume of a speaker's voice in a lar: Volume belongs to spoken speech. Written tone is shown through words.
ww.The length of the message in words on th: Length is how long a message is. It is not what tone means.

rw: A formal business letter has a proper greeting, a clear body and a courteous closing. This structure shows respect and makes the message easy to follow.

ww.Slang, emojis and abbreviations througho: Slang, emojis and abbreviations are too casual for a formal letter. They would look unprofessional.
ww.A single run-on sentence without any pun: A run-on sentence without punctuation is hard to read. It is not suitable for a formal letter.
ww.Only a subject line with no content at a: A subject line alone has no content. A letter needs a message.

rw: Offering a close alternative or a special order helps the customer. It keeps the sale and builds loyalty.

ww.Say that the store never sells anything: Saying the store never sells anything like it is rude and may be untrue. It ends the conversation without helping.
ww.Ask the customer to stop asking for unus: Telling customers to stop asking is dismissive. Their requests show what they want.
ww.Walk away to help someone else without g: Walking away leaves the customer without help. It shows poor service.

rw: Personalizing service means tailoring interactions to a customer's needs and preferences. It makes customers feel valued.

ww.Using the same script with every custome: Using the same script for all customers is the opposite of personalizing. It ignores the person.
ww.Giving every single customer identical o: Identical offers for everyone are impersonal. Personalizing means matching what each customer wants.
ww.Refusing to remember any of the returnin: Refusing to remember returning customers ignores them. Personalizing uses what you know about them.

rw: Confirming that the issue is fixed and thanking the guest shows care. It completes the recovery and keeps goodwill.

ww.Assume the problem is solved and avoid t: Assuming it is solved and avoiding the guest does not confirm the issue. The guest may still be unhappy.
ww.Argue that the room was already clean wh: Arguing blames the guest. It damages the relationship.
ww.Charge the guest an extra cleaning fee f: Charging an extra fee for a problem the hotel caused is unfair. It would anger the guest.

rw: Word of mouth is valuable because customers trust recommendations from people they know. Friends and family are more credible than ads.

ww.It cannot be changed by the quality of t: Word of mouth depends on service quality. Great service gets good reviews and poor service gets bad ones.
ww.It works only through paid ads in the ne: Word of mouth is not paid advertising. It spreads between customers freely.
ww.It costs more than any other kind of adv: Word of mouth costs little or nothing. It is often cheaper than other advertising.

rw: Customer lifetime value is the total profit expected from a customer over time. It helps firms decide how much to spend to win and keep customers.

ww.The number of years that a customer has: The years someone has lived in a town have nothing to do with the value of a customer. It is a profit measure.
ww.The price paid for one single purchase a: One purchase price is a single sale. Lifetime value looks at all purchases over time.
ww.The cost of acquiring one new customer a: Acquisition cost is what it costs to win a customer. Lifetime value is the profit expected from them.

rw: The law of supply states that producers offer more of a product at higher prices. A higher price makes producing more worthwhile.

ww.Producers offer less of a product at hig: The law of supply says producers offer more at higher prices, not less. Higher prices make selling more profitable.
ww.Prices never change when supply changes: Prices do change when supply changes. The law links price and quantity supplied.
ww.Buyers purchase more when prices rise in: Buyers buying more when prices rise is not the law of demand. Demand usually falls as prices rise.

rw: An increase in consumers' income raises demand for a normal good. It shifts the demand curve to the right.

ww.A fall in the price of the product itsel: A fall in the product's own price moves along the demand curve. It does not shift the curve.
ww.A decrease in the number of buyers in th: Fewer buyers lowers demand. It shifts the curve to the left.
ww.A rise in the cost of raw materials for: Higher costs of raw materials affect supply. They do not shift the demand curve.

rw: When supply falls, the price rises and the quantity sold falls. Less coffee is available, and buyers pay more.

ww.The price rises and the quantity sold ri: A bad harvest cuts supply, so the price rises. Quantity sold would fall, not rise.
ww.The price falls and the quantity sold ri: Falling price and rising quantity would follow a rise in supply. A bad harvest causes the opposite.
ww.Neither price nor quantity changes at al: Supply shocks change the market. Price and quantity change after a bad harvest.

rw: A monopoly is a market with a single seller and no close substitutes. The seller has power over price.

ww.A market with many sellers of the same p: Many sellers of the same product describe perfect competition. A monopoly has one seller.
ww.A market with two equal sellers of the s: Two equal sellers form a duopoly. A monopoly has just one.
ww.A market where only the buyers set the p: In a monopoly, the seller has the power to set price. Buyers do not set it.

rw: A recession is a period of declining economic activity lasting several months. Output, jobs and spending fall.

ww.A time when all prices fall to zero in t: Prices do not fall to zero in a recession. A recession is a decline in economic activity.
ww.A one-day fall in a stock price on an ex: A one-day fall in a stock price is a market move. A recession lasts months.
ww.A period of rapid economic growth and lo: Rapid growth and low unemployment describe an expansion. It is the opposite of a recession.

rw: When demand is elastic, a price rise causes a larger percentage fall in quantity. Total revenue falls because the drop in sales outweighs the higher price.

ww.Total revenue doubles automatically in t: Revenue does not double. A price rise on elastic demand lowers quantity sold more than it raises price.
ww.Total revenue rises because each custome: Revenue rises on a price rise only when demand is inelastic. With elastic demand, customers cut back sharply.
ww.Total revenue stays exactly the same as: Revenue changes after a price rise. With elastic demand it falls.

rw: Noticing their mood and asking if they want to talk shows social awareness. It reads their feelings and offers support.

ww.Joking about the setback in front of the: Joking about a setback in front of the team hurts the person. It shows no awareness of their feelings.
ww.Telling them to stop being sensitive abo: Telling them to stop being sensitive dismisses their feelings. Social awareness means noticing others' emotions.
ww.Pretending nothing is wrong at the meeti: Pretending nothing is wrong ignores their feelings. Social awareness picks up on others' moods.

rw: Self-motivation is the inner drive to pursue goals without constant outside pressure. It keeps people working through setbacks.

ww.Working only when a reward is guaranteed: Working only for a guaranteed reward depends on outside incentives. Self-motivation comes from within.
ww.Avoiding challenging tasks at work whene: Avoiding challenging tasks shows low drive. Self-motivated people take on challenges.
ww.Waiting for a supervisor to give each in: Waiting for instructions shows dependence. Self-motivation means acting on your own.

rw: Pausing, asking clarifying questions and looking for useful points shows emotional intelligence. It manages the defensive reaction and learns from feedback.

ww.Complaining about the person who gave th: Complaining about the person to coworkers spreads negativity. It does not use the feedback.
ww.Immediately arguing back with the person: Arguing back immediately lets emotion lead. It damages the relationship.
ww.Ignoring the feedback and carrying on as: Ignoring the feedback misses a chance to improve. Strong emotional intelligence uses feedback.

rw: Active listening shows the speaker that their views are valued. People trust those who pay attention and respect what they say.

ww.It lets the listener control the whole c: Active listening does not control the conversation. It gives the speaker room to talk.
ww.It prevents the speaker from sharing det: Active listening encourages the speaker to share. It does not prevent details.
ww.It replaces the need to respond to the s: Active listening does not replace responding. A good listener also replies thoughtfully.
